_what: Section 07: the argument over Planet Nine as a ledger, one row per paper, year by year. Lanes: for a planet, against one, data and searches (which may branch toward a side), and what comes next.
_caution: 'lane' and 'branch' are our editorial reading of what each paper does to the argument, like 'stance' in papers.json. Say so on the site.
Entries with a 'doi' take their title, authors, citation count and links from papers.json; 'title' and 'line' here are a one- or two-line retelling of that paper's abstract-checked summary.
'excluded' percentages are the fractions of the predicted parameter space an empty search ruled out, quoted from the paper's abstract.
'diagram' names a drawing in src/charts/fieldart.js. The drawings are schematic: they show the kind of claim, not measured orbits.
'photos' are small inline portraits from Wikimedia Commons; scripts/fetch_portraits.py downloads them and fills in 'credit', 'license' and 'source' from the Commons API.
'next' entries describe searches that are under way or proposed. They are not findings.

_lanes.for: argues the pattern is real and a planet is the best explanation
_lanes.against: argues the pattern is a selection effect, or that something other than a planet explains it
_lanes.data: a new object, a constraint, a search or a survey; branches toward a side only when its authors draw that conclusion
_lanes.next: a search that is running or planned, and what it could settle

entries.title: A second Sedna is found
entries.line: 2012 VP113 never comes within 80 AU of the Sun. Only Sedna was known on such a detached orbit (Trujillo & Sheppard).

branch.text: Its discoverers notice that the distant orbits point the same way, and suggest an unseen super-Earth could be holding them there.

entries.title: Nothing Saturn-sized within 28,000 AU
entries.line: WISE scanned the whole sky in infrared and found no companion (Luhman, Penn State). A planet of a few Earth masses is far too faint for it.

entries.title: Six aligned orbits point to a planet of ten Earth masses
entries.line: Batygin and Brown (Caltech) reproduce the alignment in simulations with a distant planet on an opposing orbit, and name it Planet Nine.

photos.commons: File:Konstantin Batygin by Christopher Michel in 2022 01.jpg

entries.title: Saturn's position rules out some directions
entries.line: Cassini's ranging to Saturn would have felt a massive planet nearby. Fienga and Laskar cross those directions off; the rest stay open.

entries.title: The longest orbits beat in simple ratios, as if resonant with a planet near 665 AU
entries.line: Malhotra, Volk and Wang (Arizona): an independent argument that lands near the same planet.

entries.title: The clustering may be where telescopes happened to look
entries.line: OSSOS tracked exactly where it pointed and how deep it saw. Its own eight distant objects show no clustering at all.

entries.title: An orbit tilted 54 degrees is found
entries.line: 2015 BP519, from the Dark Energy Survey: by one measure the most extreme object known.

branch.text: Hard to explain without a massive distant perturber, judge Becker and the DES team: the first of a predicted population of tilted orbits.

entries.title: No planet needed: the distant bodies can align themselves
entries.line: A self-gravitating swarm tilts and clusters under its own gravity (Madigan and colleagues, Colorado).

entries.title: After modelling the biases, the alignment is still a 1-in-500 fluke
entries.line: Brown and Batygin; their review the same year shrinks the planet to 5 to 10 Earth masses on a closer orbit.

entries.title: Three bias-tracked surveys see no significant clustering
entries.line: 14 objects from DES, OSSOS and the Sheppard–Trujillo survey are consistent with random orientations (Napier and colleagues, Michigan).

entries.title: A refined fit: 6 Earth masses at 380 AU, and a map of where to look
entries.line: Brown and Batygin keep the clustering significant at 99.6%. The planet comes out closer and brighter than first thought.

photos.commons: File:Konstantin Batygin by Christopher Michel in 2022 01.jpg

entries.title: No heat signal in millimetre waves
entries.line: The Atacama Cosmology Telescope searched 18,000 square degrees blind. Ten weak candidates, none convincing.

excluded.text: ruled out for a 5 Earth-mass planet (9% for 10)

entries.title: ZTF sees nothing to magnitude 20.5
entries.line: The planet's own proponents search the Zwicky Transient Facility archive and come up empty.

excluded.text: of the predicted planets ruled out

entries.title: Pan-STARRS1 sees nothing to magnitude 21.5
entries.line: With ZTF and DES, most of the predicted planets are gone. What remains is faint and near the Milky Way's plane.

excluded.text: of the predicted planets now ruled out

entries.title: One infrared source moved the right amount
entries.line: Phan, Goto and colleagues compare the IRAS and AKARI sky surveys, 23 years apart. Two detections cannot fix an orbit.

branch.text: If real: 500 to 700 AU out and 7 to 17 Earth masses. It stays a candidate until someone follows it up.

entries.title: A fourth Sedna-like object, Ammonite, is found
entries.line: 2023 KQ14 (Subaru Telescope): perihelion 66 AU, stable for 4.5 billion years.

branch.text: Its orbit points the other way from the rest. A planet, if there is one, must sit farther out, near 500 AU.

entries.title: A dwarf planet on an 830 AU orbit, outside the cluster
entries.line: 2017 OF201, about 700 km across, found by Cheng, Li and Yang (IAS and Princeton). Posted May 2025, published 2026.

branch.text: Its perihelion direction falls outside the clustering: a challenge, the authors say, to the dynamical evidence.

entries.title: Rubin's ten-year survey begins
entries.line: The Legacy Survey of Space and Time started on 29 June 2026. By October its pipelines had found a probable dwarf planet, 2026 ED138.

links.label: SLAC: first dwarf planet candidate (27 Oct 2026)

entries.title: Find it, or empty most of the remaining space
entries.line: Most predicted brightnesses are within reach of a single Rubin image (Brown & Batygin 2021). A few years of data decide.

entries.title: A few deep images could settle the infrared candidates
entries.line: DECam or Subaru pointings along the predicted tracks would confirm or dismiss them.

entries.title: Listen for its heat with the Simons Observatory
entries.line: Same Chilean plateau as ACT, far more sensitivity: a planet's own warmth, independent of reflected sunlight.

entries.title: Every new distant orbit is a vote
entries.line: Rubin should find tens of thousands of trans-Neptunian objects. If they cluster, the case grows; if they scatter, it fades.
